subject: math
title: Data and Statistics: Center, Spread, Graphs, Probability, and Counting
objectives: Students will find the mean, median, mode, and range of a data set, and find a missing value when the mean is given.
Students will compute a weighted average and explain why it differs from a simple average.
Students will read and interpret bar graphs, line graphs, circle graphs, and tables to answer questions and compare values.
Students will find the probability of simple events and of compound events, with and without replacement.
Students will count outcomes using the fundamental counting principle and tell when order matters (permutations) and when it does not (combinations).
teach:
Objectives

  • Find the mean, median, mode, and range of a data set, and find a missing value when the mean is known.
  • Compute a weighted average.
  • Read bar graphs, line graphs, circle graphs, and tables accurately.
  • Find simple and compound probabilities, with and without replacement.
  • Count outcomes with the fundamental counting principle; distinguish permutations from combinations.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen
  • Printed or digital copies of this week's Student Lesson and Study Sheet
  • Scratch paper and pencils
  • An on-screen or handheld scientific calculator (allowed for most of today's work; the no-calculator warm-up builds mental math)
  • Optional: a coin, two number cubes, and a small bag of colored chips or paper slips for probability demonstrations

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Five quick problems on averages, ordering, percents, and multiplying.
Direct instruction20Measures of center and spread, including the missing-value method (7 min); weighted average (3 min); reading graphs and tables (3 min); probability (4 min); counting (3 min).
Guided practice15Six problems worked with the class, one from each skill.
Independent practice15Students start the 12 weekly practice items (items 1–8 in class; finish at home).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding, preview of the exit ticket, and this week's study plan.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Post these as students arrive. No calculators.

  1. What is the average of 10, 20, and 30?
  2. Put in order from least to greatest: 14, 9, 21, 9, 17
  3. What is 25% of 80?
  4. If you flip a coin, what is the chance it lands heads up?
  5. 3 × 4 × 2

Answers: (1) 20   (2) 9, 9, 14, 17, 21   (3) 20   (4) 1/2   (5) 24

Each warm-up problem previews a skill: (1) the mean, (2) sorting for the median, (3) circle graphs, (4) probability, and (5) the counting principle. Point out that in problem 2 the number 9 appears twice; you will call that the mode in a few minutes.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes)

1. Measures of center and spread (about 7 minutes)

Talking points:

  • A data set is a list of numbers about one thing: test scores, daily tips, commute times. We describe it with a “typical” value (center) and how spread out it is.
  • Mean (average): add all the values, then divide by how many values there are.
  • Median: the middle value after you sort the list. With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.
  • Mode: the value that appears most often. A set can have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode (if no value repeats).
  • Range: greatest value minus least value. It measures spread, not center.
  • An outlier (a value far from the rest) pulls the mean toward it but barely moves the median. That is why reports of home prices or incomes often use the median.
  • Missing value from a mean: mean × number of values = total. Subtract the values you know from the total to find the missing one.

Worked Example 1 (center and spread). A server's tips for six evenings were $42, $55, $38, $61, $55, and $49. Find the mean, median, mode, and range.

Mean: 42 + 55 + 38 + 61 + 55 + 49 = 300; 300 ÷ 6 = $50

Median: sort first: 38, 42, 49, 55, 55, 61. Six values, so average the 3rd and 4th: (49 + 55) ÷ 2 = 104 ÷ 2 = $52

Mode: 55 appears twice; every other value appears once. Mode = $55

Range: 61 − 38 = $23

Worked Example 2 (missing value from a mean). Luis has quiz scores of 72, 85, and 78. What score does he need on the fourth quiz so that his mean for all four quizzes is 80?

Total needed: 80 × 4 = 320

Total so far: 72 + 85 + 78 = 235

Missing score: 320 − 235 = 85

Check: (72 + 85 + 78 + 85) ÷ 4 = 320 ÷ 4 = 80. Correct.

Point out the trap: some students average the three scores (78.33) and then try to “average up” to 80. Always go through the total.

2. Weighted average (about 3 minutes)

Talking points:

  • A weighted average is used when some values count more than others: course grades with percentages, prices of different amounts, or group averages with different group sizes.
  • Method: multiply each value by its weight, add the products, then divide by the total weight. If the weights are percents that add to 100%, just add the products (no division needed).

Worked Example 3 (weighted average). In a course, tests count 50%, homework counts 20%, and the final exam counts 30%. Dee's test average is 80, her homework average is 95, and her final exam score is 70. What is her course grade?

Tests: 0.50 × 80 = 40

Homework: 0.20 × 95 = 19

Final: 0.30 × 70 = 21

Course grade: 40 + 19 + 21 = 80

The simple average (80 + 95 + 70) ÷ 3 ≈ 81.7 is wrong because it treats homework as if it counted as much as tests.

3. Reading graphs and tables (about 3 minutes)

Talking points:

  • Before answering anything, read the title, the axis labels, the units, and the scale (how much each gridline is worth). Many wrong answers come from skipping this step.
  • Bar graphs compare amounts across categories. Line graphs show change over time; a steeper segment means a bigger change. “Greatest increase” means the steepest upward segment.
  • Circle graphs show parts of a whole, usually as percents that add to 100%. To find an amount: percent × total. Each section's angle is percent × 360°.
  • Tables: find the row and column first, then read the cell. Check whether numbers are in thousands, percents, or other units.

Worked Example 4 (circle graph). A circle graph shows how a family spends its $3,200 monthly income: Housing 30%, Food 15%, Transportation 12%, Savings 10%, Other 33%. How much goes to food and transportation together?

Combined percent: 15% + 12% = 27%

Amount: 0.27 × 3,200 = $864

Check the parts: 0.15 × 3,200 = 480 and 0.12 × 3,200 = 384; 480 + 384 = 864.

4. Probability (about 4 minutes)

Talking points:

  • Probability of an event = (number of favorable outcomes) ÷ (total number of possible outcomes), when all outcomes are equally likely.
  • Probability is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain). It can be written as a fraction, decimal, or percent.
  • P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
  • Compound “and” events: multiply. For independent events (a coin and a number cube, or drawing with replacement), the probabilities do not change. For dependent events (drawing without replacement), reduce both the favorable count and the total for the second draw.

Worked Example 5 (simple and compound probability).

(a) A number cube is rolled. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4? Favorable: 5 and 6 (2 outcomes). Total: 6. P = 2/6 = 1/3.

(b) A coin is flipped and a number cube is rolled. What is P(heads and an even number)? P(heads) = 1/2; P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2. Independent, so multiply: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

(c) A box holds 8 batteries; 2 are dead. Two are chosen without replacement. What is P(both dead)? First: 2/8. After one dead battery is removed, 1 dead battery remains out of 7. P = 2/8 × 1/7 = 2/56 = 1/28.

5. Counting (about 3 minutes)

Talking points:

  • Fundamental counting principle: if one choice can be made in m ways and a second in n ways, both together can be made in m × n ways. Extend to any number of choices.
  • Permutation (order matters): arranging or assigning different roles. 5 runners finishing 1st, 2nd, 3rd: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.
  • Combination (order does not matter): choosing a group. Count the ordered ways, then divide by the number of ways to arrange the group. Choosing 3 of 5 runners for a relay team: 60 ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 60 ÷ 6 = 10.
  • Ask: “If I swap two people, is it a different result?” If yes, order matters.

Worked Example 6 (counting). A uniform has 3 shirt colors, 4 pant styles, and 2 shoe types. How many uniforms are possible? 3 × 4 × 2 = 24.

A club of 6 members picks a president and a treasurer (different people). Order matters: 6 × 5 = 30.

The same club picks 2 members to attend a conference. Order does not matter: 30 ÷ 2 = 15.

Teacher note: If time is short, model Examples 1, 2, 5, and 6 fully and assign Examples 3 and 4 as quick think-alouds. The missing-value method (Example 2) and the “and means multiply” rule (Example 5) appear on the GED often, so do not skip them.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Give students about two minutes per problem, then have a volunteer explain each step aloud while you write.

  1. Find the mean, median, mode, and range of 8, 3, 11, 5, 8.
  2. The mean of five numbers is 12. Four of the numbers are 10, 15, 9, and 14. What is the fifth number?
  3. Class A has 20 students with a mean score of 78. Class B has 30 students with a mean score of 88. What is the mean score of all 50 students?
  4. In a survey, 40 people named their favorite fruit: apples 12, bananas 8, grapes 15, oranges 5. What percent chose grapes? If the results were shown on a circle graph, how many degrees would the grapes section be?
  5. A spinner has four equal sections numbered 1 to 4. You spin it once and flip a coin. What is P(3 and tails)?
  6. Eight people enter a contest. In how many ways can 1st and 2nd prizes be awarded? In how many ways can 2 people be chosen as co-winners?

Answers with steps:

1. Sum: 8 + 3 + 11 + 5 + 8 = 35; mean = 35 ÷ 5 = 7. Sorted: 3, 5, 8, 8, 11; median = 8. Mode = 8. Range = 11 − 3 = 8.

2. Total: 12 × 5 = 60. Known: 10 + 15 + 9 + 14 = 48. Fifth number: 60 − 48 = 12.

3. Class A total: 20 × 78 = 1,560. Class B total: 30 × 88 = 2,640. Combined: 1,560 + 2,640 = 4,200; 4,200 ÷ 50 = 84. (Not 83, the simple average of 78 and 88, because Class B is larger.)

4. 15 ÷ 40 = 0.375 = 37.5%. Angle: 0.375 × 360° = 135°.

5. P(3) = 1/4 and P(tails) = 1/2. Multiply: 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8.

6. Ordered: 8 × 7 = 56. Unordered: 56 ÷ 2 = 28.

Independent Practice (15 minutes)

Students open this week's 12 practice items and complete items 1–8 in class. Items 9–12 (counting, weighted average, compound probability, and permutations versus combinations) are the harder multi-step problems; students finish them at home. Circulate and look at scratch work: did they sort before finding the median? Did they divide by the right count? Before giving a hint, ask, “What is the total you need?” or “Does order matter here?”

Checks for Understanding

  • Which measure of center is most affected by one very large value? Expected: the mean.
  • What is the median of 2, 4, 4, 10? Expected: 4 (the average of the two middle values, 4 and 4).
  • Can a probability be 1.3? Expected: no; probabilities are between 0 and 1.
  • Two cards are drawn without replacement. Does the second probability change? Expected: yes; the total (and maybe the favorable count) goes down by one.
  • Does order matter when choosing a president and a vice president? When choosing two people for a committee? Expected: yes for officers (permutation); no for a committee (combination).

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Finding the median without sorting. For 9, 2, 7, a student says the median is 2 (the middle of the list as written). Correction: always rewrite the list in order first: 2, 7, 9, so the median is 7.

Dividing by the wrong count. Students divide by the number of different values, or forget a repeated value. Correction: count every value in the list, including repeats, before dividing.

Treating a weighted average as a simple average. Correction: ask, “Do all the values count equally?” If not, multiply each value by its weight first.

Misreading a graph's scale. Students assume each gridline is 1 when it is 5 or 20, or they read the wrong bar. Correction: before answering, have students say aloud what one gridline is worth and trace from the top of the bar straight across to the axis.

Adding instead of multiplying for “and.” For P(heads and 6), a student writes 1/2 + 1/6. Correction: “and” with independent events means multiply: 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12. A combined event cannot be more likely than either part.

Ignoring “without replacement.” Students use the same fraction twice. Correction: physically remove a chip from the bag and recount before the second draw.

Adding choices instead of multiplying. With 3 shirts and 4 pants, a student says 7 outfits. Correction: list a few outfits for one shirt (4 of them), then ask how many shirts there are.

Differentiation

Support: Have students write each data set in order on a fresh line before doing anything else. Provide a step card: “Mean: add, count, divide. Median: sort, find middle. Mode: most often. Range: biggest minus smallest.” For probability, use real chips in a bag and a tree diagram for two-step events. For counting, make an organized list for small cases before using multiplication.

Stretch: Ask: “The mean of 6 numbers is 15. When one number is removed, the mean of the rest is 14. What number was removed?” (6 × 15 = 90; 5 × 14 = 70; removed 90 − 70 = 20.) Then: “From 10 people, how many 3-person committees are possible?” (10 × 9 × 8 = 720; 720 ÷ 6 = 120.)

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Ask two or three checks for understanding. Each student states one rule to remember (for example, “sort before you find the median” or “and means multiply”). Preview the Post Lesson exit ticket and this week's study plan, including this week's Practice GED.

How This Shows Up on the GED

  • Data questions. Expect tables, bar graphs, line graphs, circle graphs, scatter plots, and dot plots. Questions ask for a value read from the graph, a difference or percent, the greatest change, or which statement is supported by the data.
  • Question formats. Multiple choice; fill-in-the-blank (“What is the median?”); drop-down (“The mean is greater than / less than / equal to the median”); drag-and-drop (match each measure to its value); select-two items about which statements are true.
  • Typical wording. “What score must she earn on the next test to have a mean of 85?” “What is the probability that both items selected are defective?” “How many different combinations are possible?” “Between which two months did the greatest increase occur?”
  • Built-in traps. Wrong choices match the median when the mean is asked, the range when the mean is asked, the simple average when a weighted average is needed, and the with-replacement answer when the problem says without replacement.
  • Tools. The calculator is available for most of the test, but the formula reference sheet gives only brief definitions of the mean and the median; it does not cover the mode, the range, weighted averages, probability, or counting, so students must know those rules by heart.
student:
Welcome to Week 4

Data is everywhere: paychecks, grocery receipts, sports scores, weather reports, and news graphs. This week you will learn to describe a set of numbers, read graphs carefully, find the chance that something happens, and count possibilities quickly. These skills appear on the GED math test and also on the Science and Social Studies tests. Write every step on paper.

1. Mean, Median, Mode, and Range

  • Mean (average): add all the values, then divide by how many values there are.
  • Median: put the values in order. The median is the middle value. If there is an even number of values, the median is halfway between the two middle values (add them and divide by 2).
  • Mode: the value that appears most often. There can be more than one mode, or none.
  • Range: the greatest value minus the least value. It tells how spread out the data are.

Example 1. Seven workers' commute times (in minutes) are 25, 40, 30, 25, 35, 45, and 52. Find the mean, median, mode, and range.

Mean: 25 + 40 + 30 + 25 + 35 + 45 + 52 = 252; 252 ÷ 7 = 36 minutes

Median: in order: 25, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 52. The 4th value is in the middle: 35 minutes

Mode: 25 appears twice: 25 minutes

Range: 52 − 25 = 27 minutes

Key idea: One very large or very small value (an outlier) pulls the mean toward it but hardly changes the median.

2. Finding a Missing Value When You Know the Mean

Use this fact: mean × number of values = total.

  1. Multiply the mean you want by the number of values to get the total you need.
  2. Add the values you already have.
  3. Subtract: the difference is the missing value.

Example 2. Ana bowled 132, 148, 155, and 141 in her first four games. What must she score in the fifth game to have a mean of 145 for all five games?

Total needed: 145 × 5 = 725

Total so far: 132 + 148 + 155 + 141 = 576

Missing score: 725 − 576 = 149

Check: 725 ÷ 5 = 145.

3. Weighted Average

When some values count more than others, use a weighted average: multiply each value by its weight, add the results, and divide by the total weight.

Example 3. Kim worked 30 hours at $16 per hour and 10 hours at $24 per hour. What was her average pay per hour?

Pay at $16: 30 × 16 = $480

Pay at $24: 10 × 24 = $240

Total pay: 480 + 240 = $720. Total hours: 30 + 10 = 40

Average: 720 ÷ 40 = $18 per hour

The simple average of $16 and $24 is $20, but that is wrong because she worked many more hours at $16.

4. Reading Graphs and Tables

Before you answer, check four things: the title, the labels on each axis, the units, and the scale (what each gridline is worth).

  • Bar graphs compare amounts. Read straight across from the top of a bar to the scale.
  • Line graphs show change over time. The steepest upward segment is the greatest increase.
  • Circle graphs show parts of a whole as percents. Amount = percent × total.
  • Tables: find the correct row and column, and check the units.

Example 4. A circle graph shows the favorite sports of 200 people surveyed. The football section is labeled 45%. How many people chose football?

0.45 × 200 = 90 people

5. Probability

Probability = (number of favorable outcomes) ÷ (total number of outcomes). It is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain). The probability that something does not happen is 1 minus the probability that it does.

For two events that both happen (“A and B”), multiply their probabilities.

  • Independent events do not affect each other (flipping a coin twice, or drawing and putting the item back).
  • Dependent events do affect each other (drawing without putting the item back). For the second draw, there is one fewer item in total.

Example 5.

(a) Roll a number cube (1 to 6). P(greater than 4) = 2/6 = 1/3 (the outcomes 5 and 6).

(b) Flip a coin twice. P(two heads) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

(c) A bag has 3 red and 2 blue chips. Draw two without replacement. P(both red) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10.

Watch out: Read whether the problem says “with replacement” or “without replacement.” Without replacement, both the total and the favorable count can change for the second draw.

6. Counting

Fundamental counting principle: if you make several choices in a row, multiply the number of options for each choice.

  • Permutation (order matters): assigning places or roles, like 1st, 2nd, and 3rd. Multiply down: 5 × 4 × 3.
  • Combination (order does not matter): choosing a group. Find the ordered count, then divide by the number of ways to arrange the group.

Example 6.

(a) A smoothie comes in 3 sizes and 5 flavors. Number of choices: 3 × 5 = 15.

(b) Four books are lined up on a shelf. Ways to arrange them: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24.

(c) Choose 2 of 4 pizza toppings. In order: 4 × 3 = 12. Each pair was counted twice (pepper-onion and onion-pepper), so divide by 2: 6.

Strategy: Ask yourself, “If I swap two of the choices, do I get something different?” If yes, order matters. If no, it is a combination, so divide out the repeats.

Try It

Work each problem on paper, then check your answer.

1. Find the mean, median, mode, and range of 12, 15, 9, 15, 19.

Show answer

Sum: 12 + 15 + 9 + 15 + 19 = 70; mean = 70 ÷ 5 = 14. In order: 9, 12, 15, 15, 19; median = 15. Mode = 15. Range = 19 − 9 = 10.

2. The mean of four numbers is 20. Three of them are 18, 25, and 14. What is the fourth number?

Show answer

Total: 20 × 4 = 80. Known: 18 + 25 + 14 = 57. Fourth number: 80 − 57 = 23.

3. Quizzes count 40% of a grade and tests count 60%. Jamal's quiz average is 90 and his test average is 75. What is his grade?

Show answer

0.40 × 90 = 36 and 0.60 × 75 = 45. Grade: 36 + 45 = 81.

4. Ten cards are numbered 1 to 10. You draw one card, put it back, and draw again. What is the probability that both cards show a multiple of 3?

Show answer

Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, so P = 3/10 for each draw. With replacement the draws are independent: 3/10 × 3/10 = 9/100.

5. A diner offers 3 soups, 5 main dishes, and 4 desserts. How many different meals of one soup, one main dish, and one dessert are possible?

Show answer

3 × 5 × 4 = 60 meals.
post:
Summary of Key Points

  • Mean: add the values and divide by how many there are. Median: sort, then take the middle (or the average of the two middle values). Mode: most frequent value. Range: greatest minus least.
  • To find a missing value: mean × number of values = total; subtract the known values from the total.
  • Weighted average: multiply each value by its weight, add, and divide by the total weight.
  • Read every graph's title, labels, units, and scale before answering. Circle graph amount = percent × total.
  • Probability = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, always from 0 to 1. For “and,” multiply. Without replacement, adjust the counts for the next draw.
  • Counting: multiply the number of options for each choice. If order matters, it is a permutation; if not, divide out the repeated arrangements to get a combination.

Exit Ticket

1. What is the median of 7, 2, 9, 4?

Show answer

In order: 2, 4, 7, 9. Middle values 4 and 7: (4 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5.5

2. Tasha scored 80 and 88 on two tests. What must she score on the third test to have a mean of 85?

Show answer

Total needed: 85 × 3 = 255. Total so far: 80 + 88 = 168. Needed: 255 − 168 = 87

3. A number cube is rolled. What is the probability of rolling a 5 or a 6?

Show answer

2 favorable outcomes out of 6: 2/6 = 1/3

4. A bag has 3 green and 5 yellow chips. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are green?

Show answer

3/8 × 2/7 = 6/56 = 3/28

5. Six people volunteer. In how many ways can a chairperson and a treasurer be chosen?

Show answer

Order matters (two different roles): 6 × 5 = 30

Reflection

  • Which was easiest for you this week: averages, graphs, probability, or counting? Which needs more practice?
  • Think of a time you saw a graph or an “average” in the news or at work. What question would you now ask about it (for example, “Is that the mean or the median?”)?
  • Look at one problem you missed. Was the error in sorting, dividing by the wrong count, reading the scale, or deciding whether order matters?

Test-taking strategy: name the measure before you compute. Data questions often list the mean, median, mode, and range of the same data as answer choices, so every choice looks like a “real” number. Before you calculate, underline the exact word in the question (mean, median, mode, or range) and write it at the top of your scratch work. After you compute, check that the number you picked answers that word, not a different one.

The greatest value minus the least value; a measure of spread.

notes:
Week 4 Study Sheet: Data, Statistics, Probability, and Counting

Center and Spread

MeasureHow to find it
MeanSum ÷ number of values
MedianSort; middle value (even count: average the two middle values)
ModeMost frequent value (can be none or several)
RangeGreatest − least

Example: 2, 4, 4, 7, 13 → mean 30 ÷ 5 = 6, median 4, mode 4, range 11.

Outliers pull the mean, not the median.

Missing Value and Weighted Average

Missing value: mean × count = total; total − known values = missing value.

Example: want mean 80 on 4 quizzes; have 72, 85, 78. 320 − 235 = 85.

Weighted average: (value × weight) + (value × weight) + …, divided by total weight.

Example: 30 h at $16, 10 h at $24: (480 + 240) ÷ 40 = $18.

Graphs and Tables

  • Read the title, labels, units, and scale first.
  • Bar graph: compare categories.
  • Line graph: change over time; steepest rise = greatest increase.
  • Circle graph: amount = percent × total; angle = percent × 360°.

Probability

  • P = favorable ÷ total, from 0 to 1.
  • P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
  • “And”: multiply.
  • With replacement: same fraction each draw.
  • Without replacement: subtract 1 from the total (and from the favorable count if it was drawn) for the next draw.

Example: 3 green, 5 yellow; P(two green) without replacement = 3/8 × 2/7 = 6/56 = 3/28.

Counting

SituationMethodExample
Several choices in a rowMultiply the options3 sizes × 5 flavors = 15
Order matters (permutation)Multiply downPresident and VP from 7: 7 × 6 = 42
Order does not matter (combination)Ordered count ÷ arrangements of the groupChoose 3 of 5: 60 ÷ 6 = 10

Top mistakes: finding the median without sorting; dividing by the wrong count; using a simple average when values have different weights; misreading the graph scale; adding probabilities for “and”; ignoring “without replacement”; adding choices instead of multiplying.

items.prompt: Renee's scores on five math quizzes were 78, 85, 92, 70, and 85. What is the mean of her quiz scores?
items.hint: Add all five scores, then divide by the number of scores.
items.explain:
Add the scores:

78 + 85 + 92 + 70 + 85 = 410

Divide by the number of scores (5):

410 ÷ 5 = 82

85 is the median and also the mode, not the mean. 22 is the range (92 − 70). 102.5 comes from dividing by 4 instead of 5.

items.prompt:
The number of hours Marcus worked each day for six days is listed below.

6, 9, 4, 8, 7, 10

What is the median number of hours?
items.hint: Put the numbers in order first. With six values, there are two middle numbers.
items.explain:
Put the values in order: 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10

There are six values, so the two middle values are the 3rd and 4th: 7 and 8.

Median = (7 + 8) ÷ 2 = 15 ÷ 2 = 7.5 hours

A common mistake is to use the list as written and pick 4 and 8 (the 3rd and 4th numbers before sorting), which gives 6.

items.prompt:
The bar graph shows the number of visitors to a public library on each weekday last week.

How many more visitors came on the busiest day than on the least busy day?
items.hint: Find the tallest bar and the shortest bar. Then subtract.
items.explain:
The busiest day is Friday, with 165 visitors (the tallest bar).

The least busy day is Tuesday, with 95 visitors (the shortest bar).

Difference: 165 − 95 = 70

45 compares Friday with Monday (165 − 120), and 25 compares Friday with Wednesday (165 − 140). 260 is the sum 165 + 95, not the difference.

items.prompt: A bag contains 5 red marbles, 3 blue marbles, and 4 green marbles. One marble is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is blue?
items.hint: Probability = number of blue marbles ÷ total number of marbles.
items.explain:
Total marbles: 5 + 3 + 4 = 12

Blue marbles: 3

P(blue) = 3/12 = 1/4

1/3 comes from comparing blue to non-blue marbles (3 to 9) instead of blue to all marbles. 3/4 is the probability of not choosing blue. 1/12 is the probability of choosing one particular marble.

items.prompt:
A small business recorded the number of online orders it received on five days:

10, 3, 13, 6, 3

Drag each measure to its value for this data set. Each value is used once.
items.hint: Sort the data first: 3, 3, 6, 10, 13. Then find each measure.
items.explain:
Sort the data: 3, 3, 6, 10, 13

Mean: 3 + 3 + 6 + 10 + 13 = 35; 35 ÷ 5 = 7

Median: the middle (3rd) value is 6

Mode: 3 appears twice, so the mode is 3

Range: 13 − 3 = 10

A common mistake is to take the middle number of the unsorted list (13) as the median.

items.prompt: Darnell's scores on his first four tests were 84, 76, 90, and 81. What score does he need on the fifth test so that the mean of all five tests is exactly 85?
items.hint: Multiply the mean you want by the number of tests to get the total you need. Then subtract the scores he already has.
items.explain:
Total needed for a mean of 85 on 5 tests: 85 × 5 = 425

Total so far: 84 + 76 + 90 + 81 = 331

Score needed: 425 − 331 = 94

Check: (84 + 76 + 90 + 81 + 94) ÷ 5 = 425 ÷ 5 = 85.

85 is the target mean, not the needed score. 87.25 comes from averaging his current mean (331 ÷ 4 = 82.75) with the fifth score as if they counted equally. 9 comes from multiplying 85 by 4 instead of 5 (340 − 331).

items.prompt:
A circle graph shows how Tanya spends her monthly take-home pay of $2,800. The sections of the graph are listed in the table.

CategoryPercent of take-home pay
Rent38%
Food20%
Transportation15%
Utilities10%
Savings8%
Other9%

How much money does Tanya spend each month on food and transportation combined?
items.hint: Add the two percents, then multiply by the total take-home pay.
items.explain:
Add the two percents: 20% + 15% = 35%

Multiply by the total: 0.35 × $2,800 = $980

Check: food is 0.20 × 2,800 = $560 and transportation is 0.15 × 2,800 = $420; $560 + $420 = $980.

$560 and $420 are each only one of the two categories. $1,820 is 65% of her pay, the amount spent on everything except food and transportation.

items.prompt:
The line graph shows the number of gym memberships a fitness center sold each month from January to June.

Choose the option that makes each statement true.

The greatest increase from one month to the next occurred between {{0}}.

The range of the monthly sales is {{1}} memberships.

The mean number of memberships sold per month is {{2}}.
items.hint: Read each month's value from the graph: each gridline is 10. An increase means the line goes up.
items.explain:
Values from the graph: Jan 40, Feb 20, Mar 30, Apr 50, May 30, Jun 10.

Greatest increase: Feb to Mar: 30 − 20 = +10. Mar to Apr: 50 − 30 = +20. Every other change is a decrease. The greatest increase was between March and April. (January to February and April to May are decreases.)

Range: 50 − 10 = 40. Choosing 50 gives only the greatest value.

Mean: 40 + 20 + 30 + 50 + 30 + 10 = 180; 180 ÷ 6 = 30. Choosing 36 comes from dividing by 5 instead of 6, and 180 is the total, not the mean.

items.prompt: A sandwich shop lets customers build a lunch special by choosing 1 of 4 breads, 1 of 6 fillings, and 1 of 3 side dishes. How many different lunch specials are possible?
items.hint: When you make one choice from each group, multiply the number of options in each group.
items.explain:
By the fundamental counting principle, multiply the number of choices for each part:

4 breads × 6 fillings × 3 sides

4 × 6 = 24; 24 × 3 = 72

13 comes from adding (4 + 6 + 3) instead of multiplying. 24 leaves out the side dishes. 216 comes from using 6 for every choice (6 × 6 × 6).

items.prompt: A coffee shop mixes 3 pounds of coffee that costs $8.00 per pound with 5 pounds of coffee that costs $12.00 per pound. What is the cost per pound of the mixture, in dollars?
items.hint: Find the total cost of all the coffee, then divide by the total number of pounds.
items.explain:
Cost of the $8.00 coffee: 3 × $8.00 = $24.00

Cost of the $12.00 coffee: 5 × $12.00 = $60.00

Total cost: $24.00 + $60.00 = $84.00

Total weight: 3 + 5 = 8 pounds

Cost per pound: $84.00 ÷ 8 = $10.50

The simple average of $8 and $12 is $10, but that is wrong because there is more of the $12 coffee in the mixture, so the cost per pound must be closer to $12.

items.prompt: A drawer contains 4 black socks and 6 white socks. Ahmed reaches in without looking and takes out one sock, keeps it, and then takes out a second sock. What is the probability that both socks are black?
items.hint: The first sock is not put back. After one black sock is removed, how many black socks and how many socks in all are left?
items.explain:
First sock: 4 black out of 10 socks, so P = 4/10.

The sock is not put back. Now there are 3 black socks out of 9 socks, so P = 3/9.

Both events must happen, so multiply:

4/10 × 3/9 = 12/90

Simplify by dividing top and bottom by 6: 12/90 = 2/15

4/25 comes from using 4/10 for both draws, as if the first sock were put back. 2/5 is the probability for the first sock only. 7/19 comes from adding the numerators and denominators (4 + 3)/(10 + 9) instead of multiplying.

items.prompt:
A neighborhood association has 7 members. All of the officer positions must be filled by different people.

Select two statements that are true.
options: There are 210 ways to choose a president, a vice president, and a secretary.
There are 35 ways to choose a 3-person planning committee.
There are 343 ways to choose a president, a vice president, and a secretary.
There are 210 ways to choose a 3-person planning committee.
There are 21 ways to choose a president, a vice president, and a secretary.
items.hint: Officer positions are different roles, so order matters. A committee is just a group, so order does not matter.
items.explain:
Officers (order matters): 7 choices for president, then 6 left for vice president, then 5 left for secretary.

7 × 6 × 5 = 210 ways. True.

Committee (order does not matter): start with the 210 ordered choices. Each group of 3 people can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 orders, and all 6 orders are the same committee.

210 ÷ 6 = 35 committees. True.

343 = 7 × 7 × 7 would allow one person to hold more than one office, which the problem does not allow. 210 committees forgets to divide out the repeated orders. 21 = 7 × 3 multiplies the number of members by the number of positions, which is not a counting rule.
